title: The instinctive synthesis
statement: The court identifies all relevant factors, discusses their significance, and at the end makes a value judgment as to the appropriate sentence from its synthesis of the factors. It is discretionary; weight cannot be allocated in advance; there is no single correct sentence, and reasonable minds may differ.

refs.q: The instinctive synthesis is where a court identifies all relevant factors, discusses their significance, and at the end of the process makes a value judgment as to the appropriate sentence given its synthesis of the factors. It is a discretionary exercise, and weight cannot be allocated to the factors in advance. The correct weight is determined by the circumstances and there is no single correct sentence.

refs.q: The instinctive synthesis is not an ‘arcane jurisprudential mantra’, but an accurate descriptor of the way a sentence is determined and is why reasonable minds may and do differ on an appropriate sentence.

refs.q: As the High Court has noted, balancing the purposes of the Act ‘is a matter of instinctive synthesis’.

title: Two-tier sentencing is prohibited (what it is, and is not)
statement: Prohibited: first identifying a 'benchmark sentence' based solely on, for example, the weight of narcotics, the maximum term, a co-offender's sentence or the scaled 'seriousness' of the offending, and then making proportional deductions from it (or then making differing orders for cumulation between co-offenders); the method has been rejected in Victoria and by the High Court. It is not a prohibition on sequential reasoning or even arithmetic deductions in certain cases.

refs.q: But it is still important to identify what two-tier sentencing means because it is not a prohibition on sequential reasoning or even arithmetic deductions in certain cases. What is prohibited is for a court to first identify a ‘benchmark sentence’, based solely on, for example, the weight of narcotics, the maximum term, a co-offender’s sentence, or the scaled ‘seriousness’ of the offending, and then make proportional deductions from that benchmark.

title: Exercising the discretion judicially
statement: The court must act reasonably and justly, according to legal principle and statute, in the public interest, not arbitrarily or by giving effect to private opinion; it must not frustrate the legislative intent, and should not attempt to remedy what it considers inadequate provision by the legislature, the executive or social institutions.

title: Procedural fairness: notice of facts and issues the sentence will rest on
statement: A court may not sentence on a fact it considers important (such as prevalence, or whether a factor is aggravating or mitigating) without identifying it and giving the parties an opportunity to address it; it cannot sentence on material not before it in open court, and error has been found where the court sought out facts or directed the prosecution to tender evidence; agreement of the parties on a point of law (such as the maximum) does not bind it; and it cannot sentence on the basis that a more serious or uncharged offence was committed, though uncharged offending may be narrative context.

refs.q: A court may not sentence an offender based on a fact it considers important — such as whether an offence is prevalent, or whether a factor is mitigating or aggravating — without first identifying the question and providing the parties with an opportunity to address the point.

statement: The prosecution may make submissions on the type of disposition but not on the range of permissible durations; such submissions were rejected by the High Court. A wrong prosecution range submission vitiates the discretion only if it influenced the court.

title: Duties of counsel relevant to the estimate
statement: Counsel must not mislead, withhold adverse authorities, stay silent on an irregularity, or fail to check the maximum penalty. The prosecution must present the facts adequately and identify comparable cases with informed submissions (a schedule alone is not enough); the court must review that material independently. Defence must identify the relevant factors and all reasonably open alternatives and adduce evidence of prerequisites for a sanction.

refs.q: More concretely, counsel must not: • mislead the court; • cast unjustifiable aspersions on a party or witness; • withhold documents or authorities that detract from their client’s case; • remain silent in the face of an irregularity; or • fail to check the maximum penalty for an offence.

title: What a guilty plea admits
statement: A guilty plea admits the essential facts of the crime but no more — not automatically the depositions or the prosecution opening. Unless legislation directs otherwise, the prosecution must establish facts beyond those admitted by the plea to the criminal standard; otherwise they cannot be used adversely.

refs.q: The plea is an admission to the essential facts of the crime, but no more, it is not automatically an admission to the facts as stated in the depositions, or the prosecution opening;

title: Fact-finding on a contested plea (Formosa) and the standard of proof
statement: The Crown opening conventionally constitutes the agreed factual basis; depositions and exhibits are the basic materials; a party wanting another matter considered must raise it and, if necessary, prove it by admissible evidence; absent a legislative direction to the contrary, facts used adversely must be established beyond reasonable doubt; facts used favourably, on the balance of probabilities. Whether a fact is adverse depends on the use made of it.

refs.q: The legal principles which apply on a contested plea hearing are the following: 1. Conventionally, the Crown opening constitutes an agreed factual basis upon which the judge passes sentence.

refs.q: 5. A sentencing judge may not take facts into account in a way that is averse to the interests of the accused unless those facts have been established beyond a reasonable doubt. title: Burden of proof and proof of mitigation
statement: The party relying on a further fact generally bears the burden. Whether a fact is adverse or favourable depends on the use made of it. title: Pre-sentence, drug and alcohol, medical and third-party reports
statement: A pre-sentence report must be ordered if the court is considering a CCO, YJC or YRC order (not for a CCO whose sole condition is less than 300 hours of unpaid work; 11.1 says “300 hours or less”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours); disputed parts cannot be relied on until the dispute is heard; the report does not control the sentence. title: Victim impact statements
statement: A victim impact statement informs the court of the crime's impact and the victim's concerns; it is not to punish the offender or produce an unjust sentence. 'Victim' means anyone who suffered injury, loss or damage (including grief, distress, trauma) as a direct result of the offence, whether or not foreseeable; it is not interpreted narrowly. If harm in the statement is disputed and would increase the sentence, causation must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Weight is for the judge; the victim's attitude cannot govern sentencing, though a favourable statement must be given appropriate weight; unsupported assertions about the victim’s attitude need not be given any weight.

refs.q: The statement is not to be used to punish the offender, to produce an unjust or unfair sentence, or to provide background and context.

title: Open court: sitting in camera needs statutory authority or a recognised exception
statement: For a court to sit in camera there must be statutory authorisation or a recognised exception; it has no inherent power to exclude the public and should not. A court may still protect confidential information (e.g. concealing witnesses’ names, not reading documents aloud), but if it sits in camera or receives unpublished documents it must say so in its published reasons.

title: A very wide discretion, exercised judicially and within the limits Parliament sets
statement: The sentencing discretion is very wide but must be exercised judicially: the court must not frustrate the legislative intent, must have regard to the scope, subject matter and purpose of legislation, and should not try to remedy what it sees as inadequate provision by the legislature, the executive or social institutions. refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.1 – Exercise of discretion

refs.q: Parliament can limit judicial discretion in sentencing, and it has done so in many ways. For example, by setting mandatory penalties for some offences, requiring a custodial term and minimum non-parole period for certain offending or against certain persons, and mandating that preconditions be satisfied before a court can make a youth justice centre order or youth residential centre order.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.1 – Exercise of discretion

title: Procedural fairness: required in all circumstances; a sentence within range is no answer
statement: Procedural fairness is required in all circumstances; relief for a breach should be refused only when it is clear the breach could not possibly have affected the sentence, and a sentence within range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness. The ultimate issue is whether there was a fair hearing (an objective test; no fault need be shown), and the key question is often what the circumstances require. Each party must have a reasonable opportunity to present its case; what is reasonable depends on the nature of the decision, the complexity of the issues and submissions, the significance of an adverse decision to the party, and the court’s competing demands.

refs.q: Procedural fairness is required in all circumstances, and relief for its breach should only be refused when it’s clear the breach could not possibly have affected the sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: The fact that a sentence falls within an appropriate range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: There are many aspects to procedural fairness, but the ultimate issue is whether there has been a fair hearing. This is an objective test and fault by the decision-maker does not need to be established.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: The key question is often what is required in the circumstances to provide a fair hearing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: What is reasonable depends on the circumstances, including: • the nature of the decision to be made; • the nature and complexity of the disputed issues; • the nature and complexity of the submissions the party wishes to make; • the significance to the party of an adverse decision; • the competing demands on the time and resources of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: An essential requirement is that each party be given a reasonable opportunity to present its case by presenting evidence or through written or oral submissions (or both) to rebut the potentially adverse determination.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: Procedural fairness is a tangible expression of the audi alteram partem rule.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: A court’s duty to afford procedural fairness is vital to the reality and appearance of justice.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

title: Notice: when the court must alert the parties
statement: If the court takes a different view of the law from the parties’ joint position (e.g. the maximum), it must say so and hear submissions. The parties cannot prevent the court obtaining further material (such as a pre-sentence report). Great care is needed before departing from agreed facts. For material not provided by the parties, the court should make doubly sure counsel have access to it or that all parties agree to its use. A change in the court’s previously expressed view of a factor should be notified. If further facts are needed and provided, a hearing must be permitted even if the plea is reopened. Where the parties agree an approach, the court must warn them not to assume it will be followed if it finds it problematic. Notice is also required where a less favourable sentence than on a previous occasion is at risk (remittal or retrial) or where the course of the plea reasonably suggests a non-custodial sentence.

refs.q: If the court determines the law to be different it must advise the parties that the joint position may not be accepted and give them an opportunity to make submissions on any issues arising from the alternate view.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: Again, the parties cannot (by their statement of agreed facts or plea agreement) prevent the court from obtaining further material – such as a pre-sentence report – necessary for it to carry out its sentencing function.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: But great care is required if a court departs from the agreed facts, and instances where error has been found in doing so include:
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: If the court has material that has not been provided by the parties, then it should make doubly sure that counsel have access to or are given copies of it, or if not, then that all parties agree the court may continue to consider the material.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: Similarly, if the court changes its previously expressed views of a factor, it should notify the parties and give them an opportunity to make submissions.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: If further facts are considered necessary and/or are requested and provided, then the court must permit a hearing on the new materials even if it requires reopening the plea.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: Where the parties agree on a particular approach to sentencing, the court must advise them they should not assume the approach will be followed if the court finds it problematic.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: The court must also put the parties on notice when there is the risk of imposing a less favourable sentence than that imposed on the offender on a previous occasion for the offence in question (such as when there is a remittal or retrial following a successful appeal), or in circumstances where it reasonably appears from the course of the plea that the offender might not be sentenced to a custodial term.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: Notice is a threshold requirement of procedural fairness and so a considerable onus exists for a sentencing court to advise the parties of varied matters and in varied circumstances.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: Similarly, the parties may agree to the facts upon which an offender is to be sentenced.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

refs.q: • A court considering facts consistently with a more serious and/or uncharged offence, rather than as essential ingredients of the charged offence to which the offender has pleaded.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

title: Unrepresented offenders: assessing what a fair hearing requires
statement: Managing unrepresented litigants requires balancing the interests of justice against the efficient use of public resources, with patience and judgment about adjournments. Where an unrepresented defendant disputes the facts, the court must be alive to the possibility that the plea is inconsistent with the dispute and should advise reconsideration. The court must assess the person’s capacity to formulate and communicate their case, and where there may be an arguable legal point they cannot articulate it should seek to elicit and clarify it.

refs.q: It requires them to balance the interests of justice with the competing public interest in the efficient use of public resources and access to justice for other litigants waiting to be heard.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: It requires patience, judgment, and the ability to determine which cases require an adjournment or prolonged hearing and those that should be disposed of expeditiously.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: Where the defendant does dispute the facts, the court must be alive to the possibility that the plea is inconsistent with the dispute, and should advise the defendant to reconsider the plea;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: In determining what is required to provide a self-represented party a fair hearing, a court will have to assess the capacity of the unrepresented person to formulate and communicate their case.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: In which case, to provide a fair hearing, the court should seek to elicit and clarify the legal point by speaking with the defendant.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

title: Disclosing concerns without apprehended bias
statement: A judge may disclose concerns about aspects of the case (failing to do so can itself deny procedural fairness), but should take care not to create a perception that it may not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind to its task: gratuitous or intemperate remarks should be avoided. Tentative views on matters the parties may then address do not show bias; the number, intrusiveness and tone of interjections may.

refs.q: This does not mean they cannot disclose concerns about aspects of the case.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: In fact there may be circumstances where the failure to do so amounts to a denial of procedural fairness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: In informing the parties of its developing views, a court should take care not to give rise to an apprehension of bias. That is, it should not create a perception that it may not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind to its task.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: To that end, a judge should avoid gratuitous or intemperate remarks as they may be taken out of context and misinterpreted.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: The expression of tentative views during argument on matters that the parties are then permitted to address does not manifest bias.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: But a greater number of judicial interjections and the degree of their intrusiveness or tone, considered within the context of the entire proceeding, may create a reasonable suspicion of prejudgment.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: As Kirby P said in Chow v DPP, ‘there is a fine line between excessive and unjudicial intervention … and candid disclosure of matters of concern to invite response’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

title: Prosecution duties at sentencing (detail)
statement: The prosecution must, among other things, correct matters put on the plea that it believes to be in error and give an adequate presentation of the facts (what is fair, reasonable and practical; not limited to the facts of the offence — e.g. criminal history and relevant post-offence conduct). The court is entitled to rely on its summaries as accurate. Unlike the defence, it cannot make unsworn, unproved assertions. A plurality of the High Court has said it may be incumbent on the prosecution to seek limiting orders for cooperation material that cannot be disclosed; other members doubt this is permissible without legislation (flag.prosecution_limiting_orders_hca_split). It must identify comparable cases (the court must review them independently), give a fair test of the defence case and help the court avoid appealable error; failure may support an appellate court’s residual discretion not to intervene on a Crown appeal. Submissions by the prosecution on the range of durations are impermissible statements of opinion (method.barbaro).

refs.q: • correcting any matters put on plea that it believes to be in error;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: An adequate presentation depends on what is fair, reasonable, and practical in the circumstances of the case, but is not limited to the facts of the offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: The court is entitled to rely on these summaries as being accurate in all matters for if they’re wrong they can lead to sentencing error.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: For example, the offender’s criminal history should be canvassed, and any relevant post-offence conduct noted.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: However, unlike defence counsel, it cannot make unproved assertions (that have not been sworn to) before the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: A plurality of the High Court has also said that in fulfilling this duty if material detailing an offender’s cooperation with authorities is offered for the court to consider any relevant discount but contains items that should not be disclosed to the accused or their counsel, then it may be incumbent on the prosecution to seek appropriate limiting orders from the sentencing court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: The court, however, must independently review that material to determine what guidance it offers;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: • providing a fair test of the defence case as required; and • assisting the court to avoid appealable error.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: Prosecution failure to meet these duties deprives the court of the assistance it is entitled to and may provide a basis for an appellate court to exercise the residual discretion not to intervene if the prosecution seeks to appeal from an error by the sentencing court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: Such submissions have been firmly rejected by the High Court as being an impermissible statement of opinion that should not be made.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: Other members of the High Court, however, seem less certain that this infringement on the open courts principle and the offender’s right to notice is permissible without legislative action;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: • informing the court of relevant sentencing law, the seriousness and circumstances of the offence, and any matters it knows are helpful to the offender;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: The prosecution’s duties at sentencing include:
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: • providing an adequate presentation of the facts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: During the sentencing hearing, the prosecution may give an oral summary of the facts, based on the written material available.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

refs.q: • identifying comparable and other relevant cases.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.1 – Prosecution

title: Defence duties: candour, and submissions for a CCO
statement: The defence must not mislead the court, affirmatively or by omission, but need not volunteer detrimental facts (such as bad character or prior convictions) unless its other submissions would mislead without them (e.g. asserting good character from an absence of priors). Arguing for a CCO requires submissions on the formulation of conditions that address the offender’s needs and the causes of the offending, not just a recital of personal circumstances.

refs.q: The defence must not mislead the court, either affirmatively or by omission. However, this does not require detrimental facts (such as bad character or prior convictions) to be put forward unless counsel’s other submissions would be misleading without disclosing such material.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: For example, if an affirmative assertion is made that the offender is of good character because they have no prior convictions, counsel would need to disclose any knowledge of the defendant’s imprisonment on post-conviction charges in another case.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: Where defence counsel wishes to argue for the imposition of a Community Correction Order (‘CCO’), it will not be sufficient to merely recite the offender’s personal circumstances.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: This requires counsel to pay attention to the formulation of conditions that will address the offender’s needs, as well as the causes of their offending, and which will promote the required changes in the offender’s life that are needed to reduce the risk of reoffending.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: • obtain the least punitive sentence properly available for their client;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: • identify the relevant sentencing factors, including those weighing in the defendant’s favour;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: During sentencing, defence counsel has a duty to: • obtain the least punitive sentence properly available for their client; • identify the relevant sentencing factors, including those weighing in the defendant’s favour; • advance argument; • tender any relevant evidence; • identify and canvas all reasonably open sentencing alternatives; • confirm or, if necessary, challenge the factual basis on which sentence is to be imposed; • present accurate information regarding rehabilitation; • consider whether to make submissions on the sentencing range; • adduce evidence to establish the factual basis on which the court might exercise its jurisdiction, where there are prerequisites for a particular sanction.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: • tender any relevant evidence;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: • confirm or, if necessary, challenge the factual basis on which sentence is to be imposed;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: • present accurate information regarding rehabilitation;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

refs.q: Counsel needs to make submissions which address the formulation of an order that directly addresses those circumstances.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.3 – Duties of counsel > 2.2.3.2 – Defence

title: The court alone decides the sentence and finds the facts; facts beyond the plea need proof
statement: The court alone decides the sentence and must find the relevant facts, subject to limits (above all, the verdict or plea). Any dispute about facts beyond the essential ingredients admitted by the plea is resolved by the ordinary criminal principles: unless legislation directs otherwise, the prosecution must establish such facts to the criminal standard, failing which they cannot be used against the offender.

refs.q: The court alone decides the sentence to be imposed and to do so it must find, subject to certain limits, the relevant facts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings

refs.q: ‘[a]ny dispute as to facts beyond the essential ingredients admitted by the plea must be resolved by the application of ordinary principles that apply in criminal cases’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea

refs.q: Absent a legislative direction to the contrary, it is the duty of the prosecution to establish any facts beyond those admitted by the plea to the criminal standard.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea

refs.q: If they do not, the court may not take those facts into account in a manner adverse to the accused.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea

refs.q: A guilty plea does two things: it is a formal and conclusive admission of the offence by the offender and it dispenses with the need for the prosecution to prove the facts that establish guilt.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea

title: Guilty pleas: obtaining an unequivocal plea; unrepresented accused; withdrawal
statement: If the court considers a plea is not genuine it must obtain an unequivocal plea or direct a not guilty plea. It should make certain an unrepresented defendant understands a guilty plea (especially where a viable defence appears) and, for a serious offence, adjourn to allow legal advice. If the evidence does not support the charge it should advise withdrawal, but it cannot compel it; if the accused refuses, the plea is final, subject to leave to change it before the matter is finalised. If an unrepresented accused insists on proceeding after an opportunity to obtain advice, the plea may be taken but set aside if circumstances later give cause for concern. When the prosecution accepts a plea, the court cannot reject it unless it is not genuine or an abuse of process.

refs.q: If the court considers the plea is not genuine it must either obtain an unequivocal plea or direct that a not guilty plea be entered.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: For this reason, a court should make certain that an unrepresented defendant really understands the effect of a guilty plea, particularly where there appears to be a viable defence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: And if an unrepresented accused is charged with a serious offence, the court should adjourn the plea to allow them to seek legal advice or consider the wisdom of doing so.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: But the court cannot compel an accused to withdraw their plea. If the accused refuses to do so, the court must consider the plea to be final, subject to its discretion to grant leave to change the plea any time before the matter is finalised.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: When the prosecution accepts a plea, the court cannot reject it, unless it is not genuine or constitutes an abuse of process.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: If an unrepresented accused insists on proceeding after being given an opportunity to seek and obtain legal advice, the court may take the plea but if any circumstances subsequently give it cause for concern the plea may be set aside.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

title: Pleas to alternative or lesser offences
statement: If a plea to a lesser alternative offence is not accepted, the trial proceeds on both counts; the plea is taken before the jury and may be used in evidence, but no conviction is recorded on the lesser offence until the verdict on the more serious one. If the plea to an alternative offence is accepted, the court is not bound by the facts that persuaded the Crown to accept it, but cannot consider aggravating circumstances that might warrant conviction for a more serious offence.

refs.q: If an accused is presented on alternative offences and offers to plead guilty to the lesser offence, but the prosecution does not accept that plea, then the trial should proceed on both counts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.2 – Proceedings after plea of guilty

refs.q: The plea should be taken before the jury, and it may be used in evidence against the accused, but the court should not record a conviction on the lesser offence until the jury has returned a verdict on the more serious offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.2 – Proceedings after plea of guilty

refs.q: If an offender pleads guilty to an alternative offence, and the prosecution accepts that plea, the court is not bound by the same facts that persuaded the Crown to accept the plea.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.2 – Proceedings after plea of guilty

refs.q: But neither can it consider aggravating circumstances that might warrant conviction for a more serious offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.2 – Proceedings after plea of guilty

refs.q: If an accused pleads guilty to only some of the charges on an indictment, and the prosecution accepts that offer then the plea is usually taken in the absence of the jury. A person arraigned on an indictment may plead not guilty to the offence charged, but guilty to a lesser offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.2 – Proceedings after plea of guilty

title: When the Evidence Act applies at sentencing; what proof contested facts need
statement: The Evidence Act 2008 does not automatically apply to sentencing. It applies only if the court so directs on a party’s application concerning proof of a fact, the court determines the proceeding involves proof of the fact, and the fact will be significant in determining the sentence; the court must so direct where appropriate in the interests of justice. Even without a direction, the law of evidence applies to contested fact finding. A contested factual assertion must be proved by admissible evidence, though not necessarily on oath or after cross-examination. Uncontested facts may be proved by admissions, agreed statements or bar-table submissions, but the court need not accept assertions that may rest on unreliable instructions.

refs.q: The Evidence Act 2008 (Vic) (‘Evidence Act’) does not automatically apply to sentencing proceedings. It only applies if the court directs that it should apply, on application of a party in relation to proof of a fact, the court determines that the proceeding does involve proof of the fact and the fact will be significant in determining the sentence. The court must also order that the Evidence Act applies if it considers appropriate to make such a direction in the interests of justice.

refs.q: A court’s refusal to direct that the Evidence Act applies does not mean the rules of evidence never apply to a sentencing proceeding.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: Even without a judicial direction under the Evidence Act, the law of evidence applies to fact finding in sentencing proceedings when the facts are contested.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: A contested factual assertion upon a plea must be proved by admissible evidence. There is, however, no requirement that the evidence should all have been given on oath, or that there should have been a prior opportunity for cross-examination.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: Uncontested facts may be proved by admissions, agreed statements or submissions from the bar table.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: But the court is not obligated to accept such assertions and should not do so if there is a risk the instructions on which they are based are unreliable.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: The Evidence Act preserves the operation of both statutory evidence law and common-law principles.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

refs.q: In Formosa v The Queen, the Court of Appeal summarised the principles that apply to fact-finding on sentencing, it said:
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence

title: Burden of proof at sentencing: who bears it, notice, and the effect of reasonable doubt
statement: There is no general burden of proof in sentencing unless a party asserts further facts; that party generally bears the burden, and the opposing party must have notice and an opportunity to be heard. Giving the offender the benefit of any reasonable doubt about adverse facts may in practice oblige the court to sentence on the view most favourable to them. Whether a fact is adverse or favourable depends on the use made of it. Failure to prove mitigation does not prove aggravation, or vice versa.

refs.q: Because the guilty plea or jury verdict have proved the facts necessary to establish the elements of the offence, there is no general burden of proof in sentencing proceedings unless a party asserts there are other facts the court must consider.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: In which case, the party calling for reliance on the further fact(s), generally, bears the burden of proof.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: The party opposing the consideration of further facts must be given notice of the intent to do so and an opportunity to be heard.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: The practical effect of the offender being given the benefit of any reasonable doubt as to adverse facts may be that the court is obliged to sentence on a view of the facts most favourable to them despite there being no explicit requirement that a court sentence in that fashion.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: There is no set rule for determining whether a fact is averse to or favours the offender. It depends on the use that the court makes of it.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: But a failure to prove the existence of mitigating circumstances does not prove the existence of aggravating circumstances, or vice-verse.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

refs.q: The consideration of any further facts, aggravating or mitigating, are subject to the requirements of procedural fairness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.1 – Burden and standard of proof

title: Proving prior convictions and subsequent offending
statement: The court must ask whether the offender admits the convictions in the criminal record; if admitted it may sentence accordingly, otherwise the prosecution may prove them (typically by an Evidence Act s 178 certificate). In the higher courts the record may be provided after the indictment is filed and before the hearing (or later in the interests of justice). In a summary proceeding where the accused is found guilty in their absence, a record served at least 14 days before may be admitted. Children’s Court orders can be proved only if made in the past 10 years. Subsequent offending cannot be proved by the CPA record process but may be admitted or proved by certificate. A conviction under appeal to the County Court may count as a previous conviction.

refs.q: In the higher courts, the record can be provided at any time after the indictment is filed and before the sentencing hearing, or if the record is not available before that time, then after the sentencing hearing commences and before sentencing if the court determines it is in the interests of justice to do so.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: The court must ask if the offender admits the convictions in the criminal record and if the offender (or their legal representative in a summary proceeding) does so the court may sentence them accordingly.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: If not, then the prosecution may lead evidence to prove the convictions, typically by obtaining a certificate under s 178 of the Evidence Act.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: In a summary proceeding, if the accused is found guilty in their absence and the court is satisfied that a copy of their criminal record was served on them at least 14 days before the hearing it may be admitted for sentencing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: Evidence of orders made by the Children’s Court relating to a person’s offending can only be given if the orders were made in the past 10 years.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: Subsequent offending cannot be proved by the CPA process just specified, but it can be admitted by the offender or proved via an Evidence Act s 178 certificate.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: If an accused is prosecuted for subsequent offending while an appeal to the County Court against an earlier finding of guilt is pending, the first conviction may constitute a ‘previous conviction’ because the notice of appeal does not stay the conviction and if the appeal is struck out because the appellant fails to appear or abandons the appeal, the original sentence is reinstated.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: An offender’s criminal record is a document that sets out all their previous convictions, and complies with the requirements of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) s 77 or s 244 (‘CPA’).
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

refs.q: The criminal record may be provided to the court by the prosecution if the offender is found guilty of a summary offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.1 – Criminal record and subsequent offending

title: Using depositions: no oath requirement; conflicts with agreed facts; co-offender material
statement: Depositions need not have been given on oath or tested by cross-examination. If they conflict with an agreed statement of facts the court should raise it with the parties. Depositions about admitted prior convictions, or a co-offender’s depositions or record of interview where parity is in issue, may be used as evidence subject to objection, but not if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.

refs.q: There is no requirement that the evidence in the depositions had to have been given on oath or that there should previously have been cross-examination.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: However, if the depositions conflict with an agreed statement of facts, the court should raise the matter with the parties.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: The court may review depositions relating to prior convictions admitted by the offender or a co-offender’s depositions or records of interview if parity is in issue. These items can be used as evidence, are subject to objection (and hearing) by the defence and should not be considered if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: However, a statement made by a person who dies before the committal is not an admissible part of the deposition.

title: Reports: distribution, disputes, drug and alcohol pre-release reports, third-party and medical reports
statement: A pre-sentence report must be filed by the specified time and copies given to the parties a reasonable time before sentencing; if distribution has not occurred the court should give time and hear submissions. If a party files a notice disputing a report, the court must not sentence on the disputed part until that party can lead evidence and cross-examine the author. Where, on receiving a drug and alcohol assessment report (itself discretionary: findings.reports), the court is satisfied the offender has a drug or alcohol dependency and the sentence is imprisonment of no more than three months followed by a CCO commencing on release, the court must then order a drug and alcohol pre-release report (prepared by an approved agency, specifying treatment; no dispute process). Unrequested third-party reports should not be considered. Medical reports are shown to the prosecutor; “without objection” does not mean the Crown concurs with their substance.

refs.q: The report must be filed with the court by the time specified and the author must provide copies to the prosecution, the offender’s legal representatives, the offender (if the court so orders), and any other person the court directs within a ‘reasonable time before sentencing’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: The court has no obligations regarding the distribution of the report, but if it learns the distribution requirements have not been complied with it should give the parties time to consider the report and provide them with an opportunity to make submissions about the report.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: Either party may a file a notice of intent to dispute any part or all of the report, and if they do the court must not sentence based on the report or part until after the disputing party has been given the opportunity to lead evidence on the disputed matter and cross-examine the author.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: On receiving a drug and alcohol assessment report, if the court is satisfied the offender has a drug or alcohol dependency and they are sentenced to a term of imprisonment of no more than three months followed by a CCO commencing upon release, the court must then order a drug and alcohol pre-release report.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: This report must be prepared by an approved agency. It is to specify the treatment the offender must undergo during the period of their CCO on release, and a copy must be provided to the offender a reasonable time before release.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: There is, however, no dispute process for this report specified by the Act.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: If the court receives a report on an offender prepared by a third-party that neither it nor any party to the proceeding has requested, it should not consider the material. Reports should only be obtained by the parties or the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: The prosecutor should be shown the report in advance and may indicate it is tendered ‘without objection’. This does not mean the Crown concurs with the substance of the report.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: Cross-examination is limited, however, to the content of the pre-sentence report, although the court may question the author.
It would be a breach of procedural fairness for the court to sentence before hearing from the party about the disputed evidence, cross-examination or submissions.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: Pre-sentence reports If the court finds a person guilty, before passing sentence it may order a pre-sentence report and adjourn the proceeding in order for it to be prepared.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: In addition to numerous specified topics, the pre-sentence report may contain any other information the author believes to be relevant or appropriate or which the court has directed to be set out.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: Once any disputes about the pre-sentence report are settled, the court may take the report into account in determining the sentence to be imposed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

refs.q: Medical reports It is common practice for defence counsel to tender medical or psychological reports during the hearing without calling the author as a witness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.3 – Reports

title: Victim impact statements: who is a victim, content, admissibility, reading aloud and weight
statement: A statement may be made on behalf of a victim under 18, incapable of making it, or not an individual. “Victim” is not read narrowly: the impact of the crime is regarded more broadly than on the immediate victim; a victim need not be the target or related to them; the harm need only be the direct result of the offence (not necessarily immediate or proximate; foreseeability is irrelevant). The statement must address only the offence of which the offender is convicted; if that impact cannot be distilled in a multi-offender, multi-charge case, it should not be admitted. The statutory admissibility regime must be observed, with some flexibility on the plea; on objection the court should rule the part inadmissible or make clear it will not be relied on. The statement is filed and served a reasonable time before sentencing. If it is to be read aloud, the court must ensure only admissible, appropriate and relevant parts are read — a mandatory obligation it cannot waive. It is one consideration only: the court may not disregard it or the victim’s attitude entirely, but that attitude cannot govern the sentence.

refs.q: The statement may be made by another person on behalf of a victim who is under 18 years of age, is incapable of making the statement, or is not an individual.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: A court should not interpret this term narrowly and must regard the impact of the crime more broadly than just its impact upon the immediate victim.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: A victim does not have to be the target of the crime or someone related to them.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The offending does not need to be immediate or proximate to the harm; there may be intervening steps.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The statement must address only the offence the offender has been convicted of. If the impact of that offence, in a case with multiple offenders and charges, cannot be distilled from the statement it should not be admitted.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The court should have clear regard for the statutory regime governing the admissibility of victim impact statements to avoid error.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: Nonetheless, subject to that obligation, reception of a victim impact statement on the plea should be approached with a degree of flexibility.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: If an objection is made to any part of a statement, the court should either rule it inadmissible or make clear – during the plea or in its reasons – that no reliance will be placed on that part of the statement.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The victim must file their statement (and any attached medical report) with the court and provide a copy to the offender or their legal practitioner, and to the prosecutor a ‘reasonable time before sentencing’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: If the request is made the court must ensure that only admissible parts of the statement that are appropriate and relevant to sentencing are read aloud and may do so by directing the person reading the statement.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: This is a mandatory obligation that the court has no flexibility to waive.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The statement is only one consideration in the sentencing process but a court may not completely disregard the statement or the complainant’s attitude towards the offender.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: But the weight to be given to the victim’s attitude varies with the circumstances of the case, and their attitude cannot govern the sentencing process in part because they may not always be able to assess what is in their own best interests.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: Some of this content may include inadmissible material. The court may exclude the entire statement, part of it, or any attached medical report if it does.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: It may however assume objection will be taken to irrelevant or inadmissible material and counsel has a duty to do so.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: They need only have suffered as a ‘direct result’ of the offending, and a person might be a victim by their mere presence in the circumstances of the crime.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: But determining if a victim has been injured ‘as a direct result’ of a particular act will sometimes involve difficult issues of causation.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: In addition to receiving viva voce evidence, a court may consider a range of materials in formulating a view of the sentencing facts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements

refs.q: Victim impact statements If the court finds a person guilty, the victim of the offence may make a statement to the court to assist it in determining the sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The victim’s statement may be in writing by statutory declaration or by statutory declaration and orally by sworn evidence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The Act’s definition of ‘victim’ makes it irrelevant whether any harm suffered by the victim was reasonably foreseeable – the only requirement is that the harm be the ‘direct result’ of the offending.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The statement details the impact of the offence on the victim and any injury, loss, or damage they suffered as a direct result of the offending.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: It may contain drawings, photos, poems or other material (including medical reports) that relates to the harm suffered.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: At the request of the prosecution, the court may call the victim, any person who made a statement on behalf of a victim, or a medical expert who made a report attached to the statement, to give evidence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: Similarly, a victim or any person who made a statement on their behalf, may call any person or medical expert to give support to any matter in the statement or medical report attached to it.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: Any person called may be cross-examined and re-examined, and any party to the proceeding may lead evidence on any matter in the statement or attached medical report.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: On application or its own motion, the court may make alternative arrangements for the examination and cross-examination of any person called.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: This may include allowing their appearance via closed circuit television or other facilities, using screens to remove them from the direct vision of the offender, permitting another person of the victim’s choice to be beside them during examination to provide emotional support, permitting only specified persons to be present, requiring practitioners not to robe, or requiring practitioners to remain seated while questioning the witness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The person making a statement may request that it be read aloud or displayed in court during the sentencing hearing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: It may be read by the person making the request, another person of their choosing who consents and the court approves, or the prosecutor.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: As with the examination of witnesses regarding the statement, the court may make similar alternative arrangements for reading the statement aloud or having it displayed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: The court itself may quote admissible parts of the statement during the sentencing hearing or in the course of sentencing the offender.
