title: Effect of a finding of guilt without conviction; what counts as a “sentence”
statement: The Act does not define “sentence”; the Criminal Procedure Act’s definition includes, among other things, reporting orders (or orders that a person is not a registrable offender) under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004, and the Court of Appeal applies it to cumulation and concurrency orders and non-parole periods. Unless an Act provides otherwise, a finding of guilt without conviction is not a conviction for any purpose, but it does not prevent other orders authorised by legislation, and it has the effect of a conviction for appeals, variation or contravention proceedings, subsequent offending and later proceedings for the same offence.

refs.q: The Act does not define ‘sentence’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: a reporting order or an order finding that a person is not a ‘registrable offender’ under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004 (Vic); and
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has held the CPA definition also applies to orders for cumulation, concurrency, and any non-parole period which is fixed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: Unless an act provides otherwise, a finding of guilt without recording a conviction must not be taken as a conviction for any purpose.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: But a finding of guilt without recording a conviction does not prevent the court from making any other order with respect to the finding that is authorised by legislation.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: And such a finding has the same effect as if a conviction has been recorded for the purposes of appeals against sentence, proceedings for variation or contravention of sentence, proceedings against the offender for subsequent offending, or subsequent proceedings against the offender for the same offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: However, the CPA does define a ‘sentence’ as including:
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: • the recording of a conviction; and
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: an order made under parts of the Act applying to custody, CCOs, fines, dismissals and etc, contraventions, superannuation, restitution, and mentally ill offenders; and
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: an impoundment or immobilisation order under the Road Safety Act 1986 (Vic) ss 84S, 84T; and
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: orders made by the Supreme or County Courts, in their original jurisdiction, relating to accountable undertakings, good behaviour bonds, fines, probation, and youth supervision orders under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (Vic) ss 365, 367, 373, 380, 387.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

title: Deferral of sentence: review, re-offending, custody and orders at the adjourned hearing
statement: When deferring sentence the court may set a review date (and reserve the review to itself); on review it may take no action or cancel the order and sentence. If the offender is found guilty of another offence during deferral, the hearing may be brought forward. The offender may be released on undertaking or bail, and a pre-sentence report may be ordered. At the adjourned hearing the court has regard to the report, the offender’s behaviour during deferral and other relevant matters; custody during deferral can be dealt with as pre-sentence detention; mandatory licence orders remain; a warrant may issue for non-appearance. The common law power to remand at large has not developed in Victoria.

refs.q: On review of a deferral order, the court may take no further action or may cancel the order and proceed to sentence the offender as if the review were the adjourned hearing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: Similarly, if the offender is found guilty of another offence during the deferral period, the court may re-list the adjourned hearing date to an earlier date and may make any order that it could have had it not deferred sentencing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: At the adjourned hearing the court determines the appropriate sentence for the offender, having regard to any pre-sentence report it ordered, the offender’s behaviour during the deferral period, and any other relevant matter.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: Any time spent in custody during the deferral period can be dealt with as pre-sentence detention.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: Any statutory obligation on the court to impose any disqualification, or make any other order in respect of the offender remain valid.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: Lastly, the court may order that a warrant to arrest the offender issue if they do not appear for the adjourned hearing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: There is also a common law power to remand an offender at large pending imposition of the sentence, but this practice has not developed in Victoria and courts should be cautious in relying upon interstate cases where it arises.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: When deferring sentence, the court may set a date – between the date of its order deferring sentence and the date of the adjourned hearing – for the offender to re-appear for review of the order.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: In deferring sentence, the court may release the offender on their undertaking to appear on the adjourned date for sentence or it may release them on bail or extend any existing bail to that date.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: It may also order a pre-sentence report regarding the offender.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: The judge or magistrate deferring sentence may further direct that any review of the order be dealt with by them.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: A sentence may be imposed for an offence in open court at any time and place in Victoria.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: The trial judge, judge receiving the plea, or another judicial officer empowered to do so, may set the time and place for sentencing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

refs.q: This includes any order cancelling or suspending a driver licence or permit or disqualifying the offender from obtaining one for any period.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.2 – Timing and deferral of sentencing

title: Formulation: time served reckoned unless otherwise directed; correcting a declaration; complex orders
statement: Where imprisonment or detention is imposed, custody in relation to the proceedings for that offence must, unless the court directs otherwise, be reckoned as time served; the period may be advised by the informant or proved, must be declared and noted, and can later be corrected if the declaration was in error. Formal orders are usually pronounced at the end of the remarks; with complex orders the court commonly states their intended effect and invites submissions before they are entered.

refs.q: If an offender is sentenced to a term of imprisonment or detention, then any period served in custody in relation to proceedings for that offence must, unless the court directs otherwise, be reckoned as time served.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: If the informant is available they may advise the court of the length of the custody. Otherwise the court may take or receive evidence on the issue.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: Later, if the court is satisfied that the period declared was in error it may correct the record and amend the sentence accordingly.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: Where the sentencing orders and directions are complex, it is common for judicial officers to indicate the intended effect of the orders and give counsel an opportunity to make submissions on whether the orders gave effect to the court’s intention before entering the orders into the records of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: There are similar provisions for young offenders sentenced to a term of detention.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: It is a discretionary matter for the court whether formal orders and directions are pronounced before or after giving reasons for sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

refs.q: In Victoria, the prevailing practice is that sentencing orders are pronounced at the end of sentencing remarks.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation

title: Multiple and mixed indictments: identifying indictments; relating State and federal orders
statement: Each of several indictments should have a unique identifying number (the court adds one if needed and announces it), and the remarks should identify which indictment each sentence relates to; after the orders the court announces the overall result. On a mixed indictment, care is needed in orders relating federal and State sentences (e.g. commencement dates) and in stating total terms.

refs.q: If the court is presented with several indictments simultaneously, each should have a unique identifying number and the court should take care to identify the indictment being addressed (and its related sentence(s)) in its sentencing remarks or when pronouncing sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.2 – Multiple indictments

refs.q: If the indictments are not uniquely identified, then the court should add an identifying alphanumeric, and should announce this for the transcript of the proceedings.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.2 – Multiple indictments

refs.q: The court should then announce the result of the various directions.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.2 – Multiple indictments

refs.q: Care must also be exercised in formulating orders which relate federal and State sentences to each other (for example commencement dates), and in indicating total terms of imprisonment where necessary.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.1 – Mixed indictments

title: Representative charges: what they permit and require
statement: A representative charge does not mean sentencing for uncharged acts: those acts are directly and highly relevant to the objective gravity of the charged offence, which is heightened because the conduct is not isolated and the impact on the victim is likely greater. It differs from taking other charges into account, rolled-up and course of conduct charges. The conduct must accurately and explicitly reflect the parties’ agreement, identified in some detail (detailed articulation is not required); if the prosecution summary reflects the agreement, the court should not go behind it. The prosecution may not use an incident charged separately, or acts outside the charged period; the essence is that the other acts cannot be particularised as separate charges. The offender’s assent must be express and unequivocal; without it, additional uncharged acts that would warrant conviction for another or more serious offence must not be treated as aggravating.

refs.q: It does not mean the offender is sentenced for uncharged acts, but rather that those acts are ‘directly and highly relevant to the objective gravity of the particular offence’ for which they are being sentenced. The gravity of the offending is heightened because the conduct in question is not isolated and because the impact on the victim is likely to be much greater.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: Consideration of a representative charge for sentencing is not the same as consideration of other charges, a rolled-up charge, or a course of conduct charge.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: The conduct stated in a representative charge must accurately and explicitly reflect the agreement between the parties. This means it must be identified with some level of detail so the whole picture can be seen, but ‘detailed articulation’ is not required.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: However, if the prosecution summary accurately reflects the agreement between the parties, the court should not ‘go behind the Crown opening’ and make its own evidentiary findings as to the basis of the plea.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: The prosecution is not allowed to rely on a specific incident that is the subject of another charge as the basis of a representative charge. The ‘essence’ of a representative charge is that the other acts cannot be sufficiently particularised to legitimately frame individual charges. Nor may it rely on acts occurring outside of the time frame specified in the representative charge.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: As indicated the parties must agree to a representative charge. It is essential that the offender’s assent be express and unequivocal. If that consent is not given and the proven circumstances do reflect additional uncharged acts, the court must not consider them as aggravating if they would warrant conviction for an additional or more serious offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: A representative charge is one of three ways in Victoria for a court to take into account other instances of uncharged offending.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

refs.q: It is approved process where there is a guilty plea as it saves time and expense for all parties.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.4 – Representative charges

title: Rolled-up and course of conduct charges: single charge, single maximum
statement: A rolled-up charge, though the court considers all its circumstances (period, number of victims, total harm), is still a single formal charge with the single-charge maximum. A course of conduct charge (a relevant sexual or fraud-related offence involving more than one incident) allows serial offending to be prosecuted where details of each instance are not available: the incidents must together amount to a course of conduct (time, place, purpose), each must be an offence under the same provision (for a sexual offence, the same complainant), and incidents need not be proved with the specificity of a single charge. It is a single offence with the substantive offence’s maximum, but the sentence must reflect the totality of the conduct, so it is likely to be higher than for one incident.

refs.q: While the court may consider all the relevant circumstances of a rolled-up charge, the pleading must still be treated as presenting a single formal charge.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.5 – Rolled-up charges

refs.q: A course of conduct charge enables the prosecution of serial offending where the specific details of any instance are not disclosed in enough detail by the evidence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: Taken together the incidents must amount to a course of conduct having regard to their time, place, or purpose of commission and any other relevant matter. Course of conduct charges are available only if each incident is an offence under the same provision and, for a sexual offence, relates to the same complainant.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: It is not necessary to prove an incident with the same degree of specificity as to date, time, place, circumstances or occasion as would be required if the offender were charged with a single incidence of the offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: A court must sentence within the maximum penalty for the charged offence but must also reflect the totality of the offender’s conduct.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: A course of conduct charge is a form of charging a substantive offence, so the maximum penalty for a course of conduct charge is the same as the maximum penalty for the relevant substantive offence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: Sentencing for a course of conduct charge is particularly difficult because it is so different from the conventional sentencing exercise.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.6 – Course of conduct charges

refs.q: Because the exercise is so difficult, the sentencing judge ‘should be given maximum assistance by way of reference to relevant sentencing materials’.

title: Commencement of sentences; CCO start; order of service
statement: A sentence generally commences on the day it is imposed (if the offender is not in custody, on arrest under the warrant). Unless otherwise ordered or legislated, imprisonment is concurrent with other uncompleted sentences. A cumulative sentence (or part) commences on completion of the sentence it is cumulated on; State cumulation needs no commencement date, but a State term imposed on a person serving a Commonwealth sentence must be directed to commence immediately after the federal term or its non-parole/pre-release period (2.4.7), or no later than that point (8.4.1) — a later date is an error on both readings; an earlier one is a caution (flag.cth_sentence_commencement_fixed_or_latest). A CCO commences on the date specified, no later than three months after the order; a CCO combined with imprisonment starts on release. A PSD declaration treats the sentence as commenced on first entering custody, but the formal commencement date is the date of sentence. Terms are served in order: terms without a non-parole period, the non-parole period, then the balance; an earlier sentence is suspended if needed to follow that order.

refs.q: Generally, a sentence commences on the day it is imposed unless the offender is not in custody, in which case it commences on the day they are arrested on a warrant to imprison for sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: It is not necessary for the court to specify the commencement date when ordering cumulation of sentences relating to State offences, but if the court imposes a term of imprisonment for a State offence on a person then serving a sentence for a Commonwealth offence, it must direct that the new State term commences immediately after completion of the federal term if a non-parole period or pre-release period was not fixed, or the end of that period if one was fixed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: A CCO commences on the date specified by the court, but no later than three months after the order is made.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: However, if the court makes a CCO in addition to imposing a term of imprisonment, the CCO does not commence until the offender’s release from prison.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: Declarations of time spent in custody before sentence result in the offender being treated as having commenced their sentence when they first entered custody for the offence. However, the formal commencement date remains the date the sentence was imposed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: If an offender is sentenced to several terms of imprisonment where non-parole periods were fixed, they must be served in the following order: any term or terms without a non-parole period; the non-parole period; and the balance of any term or terms after the end of the non-parole period, unless and until released on parole.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: If while serving a sentence, a further sentence is imposed, the first sentence must be suspended if necessary for this sequence to be followed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

refs.q: If an offender is already serving a sentence for a Commonwealth offence the court must direct when the new term commences. This must be no later than immediately after completion of the Commonwealth sentence, if no non-parole period or pre-release period was fixed, or immediately after the end of any non-parole or pre-release period fixed as part of the Commonwealth sentence.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.4 – Cumulation and concurrency > 8.4.1 – Victorian regime

refs.q: If an order for cumulation is made in respect of a sentence or any part of it, that sentence or part commences on completion of the sentence or sentences to which it is cumulative.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.7 – Commencement and order of service

note: jurisdiction mixed: the first ref also states the federal-scheme limit; the app applies only the State limb
title: Taking other offences into account (s 100): exclusions and prerequisites
statement: Treason and murder cannot be taken into account under the State scheme. Before considering pending charges the court must be satisfied that a prescribed form listing them has been prepared and given to the offender, and it is appropriate to ask whether the offender admits them and wants them considered. As a general policy the procedure should not be used to dispose of serious offences. Contested other charges are irrelevant, though admitted collateral matters may be relevant; admitted further offending may negate, reduce or qualify an inference that would otherwise mitigate.

refs.q: Treason and murder are excluded from consideration under the State scheme, and under the federal scheme the court cannot consider any indictable offence it would not have jurisdiction to try.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: Before considering the pending charges, the court must be satisfied that a prescribed form listing the offender’s other charges has been prepared and provided to the offender.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: Before passing sentence it is appropriate to ask the offender if they admit committing any or all of the listed offences and want the court to consider them in sentencing for the offences of which they have already been convicted.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: However, as general policy, this procedure should not be used for the disposal of serious offences.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: When the other charges are contested, those charges are irrelevant but matters collateral to them – such as the location of the offender, the company they were in or the conduct they engaged in – may be relevant if admitted.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: If further offending is admitted, the court may use it to ‘negate, reduce or qualify an inference as to the offender’s later conduct which would otherwise arise and operate in mitigation of sentence’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: Otherwise both regimes are similar in their requirements and operation.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

title: Reasons: when required, adequacy, statutory statements, publication and revision
statement: There is a common law duty to give reasons for sentence. Reasons are not required in every case (e.g. a routine penalty for a routine offence), but where the duty exists, failure is an error of law (though the Act provides that a failure to give reasons does not invalidate the sentence). Their extent and detail depend on the circumstances: the nature of the case, the complexity of the issues, the evidence and the parties’ submissions. Reasons may be short and need not state the obvious or identify every consideration; nor must a court always explain rejecting alternative options, particularly those not reasonably practicable. Findings should not rest on speculation. Statutory statements: the announcement before an aggregate sentence (without needing notional separate sentences); orders requiring consent or an undertaking (explaining purposes, effect, consequences of non-compliance and variation); cooperation (facts and details recorded); s 6AAA (recorded). Where legislation directs a matter be considered, it should be discussed, not merely recited. Remarks may refer to objective and informed community expectations. Where cooperation is involved, two sets of reasons (one restricted) should be published. A transcript may be revised for meaning, but not altered in substance.

refs.q: Reasons are not required in every case. For example, cases involving a routine penalty for a routine offence may not require them. But where there is a duty to provide reasons, failure to do so is an error of law.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: Reasons may be adequate even if they are very short and it is not necessary for a court to state the obvious.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: This does not mean the court must explicitly identify every thought that influenced the outcome, that failure to mention some matter means the factor was not considered, or that due weight was not given to it.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: Nor must a court always explain why it has rejected alternative sentencing options, particularly those that are ‘not reasonably practicable possibilities’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • Before imposing an aggregate sentence the court must announce, in open court and in language likely to be understood by the offender, its decision and reasons for doing so and the effect of the proposed sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: The court is not required to identify separate events giving rise specific charges and it is not required to state the sentences that would have been imposed for each offence separately, or whether they would have been imposed cumulatively or concurrently.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • Where a sanction might be imposed that has conditions which requires the offender to consent or give an undertaking. Before making the order the court must explain to the offender, in language they are likely to understand, the purposes and effect of the order, the consequences of their failing to comply with it, and the way the order might be varied.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: The facts and details of the undertaking must be noted in the record of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: These statements must be recorded in writing or otherwise.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: Where legislation directs that a matter be considered, the court should discuss it in the reasons for sentence and a recitation of the statutory language is generally considered insufficient. However, the Act also provides that a court’s failure to give reasons does not invalidate any sentence it imposed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: It should not, however, avoid references to objective and informed community expectations.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: To meet both interests, a court should publish two sets of sentencing reasons.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: The fully explained remarks should be restricted and not published beyond the parties, but the second set of reasons should be made available in the usual way.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: When a transcript of reasons for sentence is submitted to the court for revision, the court is entitled not only to correct mistakes but to alter words which do not express the intended meaning at the time the words were uttered. However, the court may not change the whole character of the reasons given in court; it must not ‘effect any alteration in substance’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: However, the findings should not be based on speculation regarding the fact.
The extent and detail of the reasons depends on the circumstances including the nature of the case, the complexity of the issues, the evidence, and the parties’ submissions.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: There is a common law duty for a court to provide reasons for sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: There are several purposes behind this requirement:
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • to ensure that an appeal may be prepared properly and in a timely fashion;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • to hold the courts accountable and protect against the arbitrary exercise of power;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • so that the parties and the public can see that justice has been done;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: • to assure the offender that they have been dealt with fairly and because they and the public have a right to know the basis of fact and the reasons why a sentencing option has been chosen.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: A similar scheme exists for Children’s Court sentencing when the court imposes a youth attendance order, a youth residential centre order or a youth justice centre order following a plea of guilty.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: A court’s sentencing remarks are a reaffirmation of societal values and these may properly be expressed in sentencing reasons.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: When a court is sentencing an offender, who is receiving a discount for cooperating with authorities, it faces two competing interests.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: The first is the need for transparency and accountability by publishing remarks that explain the reasons the sentence was imposed, and the second is the need to avoid compromising an ongoing investigation or risking the offender’s safety.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: The first fully explaining how the offender’s cooperation informed its exercise of the sentencing discretion, and the second noting the cooperation in a veiled fashion and possibly referring to the offender by a pseudonym.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

title: Correcting sentences: common law, s 104A, CPA s 412 limits, and reopening under s 104B
statement: At common law a court may correct an order to give effect to its intention but may not vary an order it intended to make. Under the Act it may amend for clerical mistakes, accidental slips or omissions, material mistakes in figures or descriptions, or defects in form (without an open-court hearing unless the interests of justice require). CPA s 412 provides very generally that a court may amend any sentence or order to correct any defect in substance or form, but it is not a “cure all”: it does not abrogate functus officio, correct substantive errors, revive an entered sentence, or apply where there was no error when pronounced. Section 104B (from 2015) allows reopening where a penalty was contrary to law or a required penalty was not imposed; the court must consider elapsed time and the consequences already suffered, and the new penalty runs from the original date unless otherwise ordered. Section 104B does not yet seem to have been tested.

refs.q: The court may not vary an order that it intended to make but the order may be corrected to give justice and effect to the court’s intention.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.1 – Common law powers

refs.q: Under the Act a court may, on application or its own motion, amend a judgment or sentence if satisfied that it contains a clerical mistake, an error arising from an accidental slip or omission, a material mistake in figures or in the description of any person, matter or thing, or a defect in form.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: This power to amend the sentence for these technical reasons does not have to be exercised in open court and the parties do not need to be heard unless the court considers it necessary in the interests of justice.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: But in DPP (Vic) v Edwards the Court of Appeal clarified this section is not a “cure all” and does not allow any error to be corrected at any time. ‘It was not intended to, and does not, abrogate the doctrine of functus officio’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: The following year the Court reiterated that s 412 of the CPA does not provide a basis for a court to correct substantive errors, specifically to recall and vary a sentence. It cannot revive a judgment, order, or sentence that has been entered into the record.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: The section has no application where the sentence did not involve error at the time it was pronounced.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: In deciding whether to exercise this power, the court must have regard to the time that has elapsed since imposing the original penalty, and in determining a new penalty it must consider the extent to which the offender has already suffered the consequences of the original penalty.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: Where the court reopens proceedings and imposes a new penalty, the new penalty is taken to have been imposed from the date of the original penalty unless the court orders otherwise.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: Parliament appears to have acted to alter that bar by providing for the reopening of a proceeding at any time in order to correct an invalid sentence, but this provision (s 104B discussed below) does not yet seem to have been tested in or employed by the courts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors

refs.q: A court may also amend its sentence if satisfied that it fails to deal with a matter that would have undoubtedly been dealt with if the court’s attention had been drawn to it.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: The Supreme Court also has the power, on application, to correct sentences of the County and Magistrates’ Courts that were beyond power.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: However, time for an appeal only starts to run when the new penalty is imposed.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: Section 412 of the CPA also provides very generally that a court may amend any sentence or order to correct any defect in substance or form.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: In response to Edwards, s 104B of the Act commenced in 2015.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: Historically, at that point it lost any power to vary the judgment, even where the sentence was wholly invalid.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors

refs.q: The only remedy had been to appeal the sentence, or to seek a writ of certiorari.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors

refs.q: A court’s common law powers remain unaffected by this part of the Act.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: The Court of Appeal may exercise this power in relation to its sentences or judgments, and for judgments or sentences that are before it on appeal or an application for leave to appeal.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: The Court considered that if the provision were read that broadly it would make s 104A of the Act pointless, which would be strange since Parliament had retained it.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

refs.q: It only provides a means for the court ‘to cure slips or mistakes’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.2 – Statutory powers

title: Sentencing in the offender’s absence
statement: A trial for an indictable offence must be conducted in the accused’s presence, including sentencing, but the court may proceed in their absence if they waive the right (absconding on bail is prima facie waiver). Reluctance to proceed where the accused absconds before trial does not mean the power to proceed to sentence will be exercised sparingly; it depends on the circumstances. If the judicial officer who imposed the sentence goes out of office or is incapacitated, and it appears probable to the Chief Justice, Chief Judge or Chief Magistrate that they will not be able to deliver sentence within a reasonable time, a second judicial officer may be nominated to do so.

refs.q: A trial for an indictable offence must be conducted in the accused’s presence. This also includes a right to be present during sentencing. But the court has the discretion to proceed in the accused’s absence if they waive their right to be present and absconding on bail is a prima facie waiver of that right.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.11 – Sentencing after retrial, in absentia, and by another judicial officer

refs.q: However, it should not be assumed that the power to proceed to sentencing will also be exercised sparingly.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.11 – Sentencing after retrial, in absentia, and by another judicial officer

refs.q: It depends on the circumstances of the case.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.11 – Sentencing after retrial, in absentia, and by another judicial officer

refs.q: If the judicial officer who imposed the sentence goes out of office or is incapacitated, and it appears probable to the Chief Justice, Chief Judge, or Chief Magistrate that they will not be able to deliver sentence within a reasonable time, a second judicial officer may be nominated to do so.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.11 – Sentencing after retrial, in absentia, and by another judicial officer

title: Open court principle
statement: Hearings should be public; sitting in camera needs statutory authority or a recognised exception (narrowly, where proceeding in public would defeat the jurisdiction). A judge should not receive sentence-relevant information in chambers. Confidential information may be protected by procedures, but closed hearings or unpublished documents must be noted in the published reasons.

refs.q: To deny the public knowledge of criminal proceedings is a grave matter, and the fundamental principle is that hearings should be public and open to view.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.1 – Open court principle

refs.q: Similarly, a judge should not receive information that has the capacity to affect the sentence in chambers.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.1 – Open court principle

refs.q: But when a court is authorised to sit in camera and does so, or where it receives documents whose content is not published, it must say so in its published reasons.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.1 – Open court principle

refs.q: For a court to sit in camera there must be a statutory authorisation or a recognised exception to the rule that court proceedings are conducted openly.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.1 – Open court principle

refs.q: There is a narrow exception to this rule if the exercise of the court’s jurisdiction would be defeated by proceeding in public. For example a court may close its doors to prevent disruption by rioters.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.1 – Open court principle

title: Judicial duties and procedural fairness: a fair hearing on any adverse information
statement: The court must exercise its discretion judicially and ensure procedural fairness: a party facing an adverse determination on any information must be made aware of it and given a reasonable opportunity to respond. A sentence within range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness; the test is objective. What is reasonable depends on the decision, the complexity of the issues and submissions, the significance to the party, and the court’s resources. For the app: any adverse matter it relies on that the user has not supplied must be surfaced as an assumption for the user to answer.

refs.q: A court has two principal responsibilities with respect to sentencing: it must exercise its discretion judicially and it must ensure the hearing is conducted in accordance with the requirements of procedural fairness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties

refs.q: It is the fundamental requirement that a party who is potentially subject to ‘an adverse determination on the basis of any information, whatever its source, must be made aware’ of the information and given an opportunity to respond.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: The fact that a sentence falls within an appropriate range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: This is an objective test and fault by the decision-maker does not need to be established.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

refs.q: • the nature of the decision to be made; • the nature and complexity of the disputed issues; • the nature and complexity of the submissions the party wishes to make; • the significance to the party of an adverse decision; • the competing demands on the time and resources of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness

title: Unrepresented offenders: the court’s special responsibilities
statement: The court must ensure an unrepresented accused understands the charge and that the plea is their decision (with the chance to seek advice), knows of bail if relevant, is informed (if the case proceeds) of the seriousness and possible penalties, can put mitigation, call witnesses and dispute facts (and reconsider a plea inconsistent with a dispute), is told of any onus to prove mitigating facts, and is invited to address relevant matters. If imprisonment is possible and no submissions are made, the court should ask about character and history.

refs.q: A sentencing court has special responsibilities when dealing with an unrepresented accused.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • informing the defendant of any onus they bear, statutory or otherwise, to prove mitigating facts;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: If an unrepresented accused makes no submissions and imprisonment is a possibility, the court should also ask them about matters of personal character and criminal history to see if there a basis for a more merciful sentence.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: A critical fair hearing question for the court to consider is whether there is or may be an arguable legal point the unrepresented defendant is unable to articulate.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • before a plea is entered, making sure the defendant understands the nature of the charge; and knows that a plea is entirely their independent decision on which they may seek legal advice and representation and may obtain an adjournment for that purpose;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • if relevant, making sure the defendant is aware of what bail is, their ability to apply for it, the matters a court considers on an application for bail, and their ability to make submissions in support of bail;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • if the case proceeds, ensuring the defendant is informed of the seriousness of the charge and all possible penalties;
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • if a plea is offered and recorded, informing the defendant of their ability to put matters in mitigation, call witnesses or produce other relevant material for the court’s consideration; and dispute or comment upon the prosecutor’s facts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: • inviting the defendant to address any areas the court feels are relevant that the defendant did not cover.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: Managing cases with unrepresented litigants is an ongoing difficulty for the courts.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: This assessment will typically be based on any written documents they have filed and where there is an oral hearing, the quality of their verbal communication.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: Having an unrepresented party file written documents in advance of a hearing is an appropriate procedure well suited to the provision of a fair hearing.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

refs.q: These include: • before a plea is entered, making sure the defendant understands the nature of the charge; and knows that a plea is entirely their independent decision on which they may seek legal advice and representation and may obtain an adjournment for that purpose; • if relevant, making sure the defendant is aware of what bail is, their ability to apply for it, the matters a court considers on an application for bail, and their ability to make submissions in support of bail; • if the case proceeds, ensuring the defendant is informed of the seriousness of the charge and all possible penalties; • if a plea is offered and recorded, informing the defendant of their ability to put matters in mitigation, call witnesses or produce other relevant material for the court’s consideration; and dispute or comment upon the prosecutor’s facts. Where the defendant does dispute the facts, the court must be alive to the possibility that the plea is inconsistent with the dispute, and should advise the defendant to reconsider the plea; • informing the defendant of any onus they bear, statutory or otherwise, to prove mitigating facts; • inviting the defendant to address any areas the court feels are relevant that the defendant did not cover.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.2 – Unrepresented offenders

title: Neutrality and apprehended bias
statement: The judge should be neutral and not inquisitorial, but may (and sometimes must) disclose concerns; tentative views that the parties can address do not show bias, but intrusive interjections may create a reasonable suspicion of prejudgment.

refs.q: At sentencing the judge or magistrate should maintain a neutral role and avoid adopting an inquisitorial position.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

refs.q: The expression of tentative views during argument on matters that the parties are then permitted to address does not manifest bias.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.3 – Apprehended bias

title: Acceptance of a guilty plea: must be free, voluntary and unequivocal
statement: A plea must be freely made and unequivocal — a true admission (not from ignorance, fear, duress, mistake or for technical advantage), though it may be partly motivated by a discount. If not genuine, the court must obtain an unequivocal plea or enter not guilty. If the evidence does not support the charge the court should advise withdrawal but cannot compel it. A plea accepted by the prosecution cannot be rejected unless not genuine or an abuse of process. For the app: if the user’s facts disclose a possible defence or deny an element, flag it — the app does not decide guilt.

refs.q: A court should not accept a guilty plea if it appears that the plea is not freely and voluntarily made.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: A guilty plea must be unequivocal and cannot be made in circumstances where it does not appear to be a true admission of guilt.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: But this does not mean a plea cannot be motivated in part by the wish to obtain a collateral benefit such as a sentencing discount or to avoid the expense of trial.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: Similarly, if the court considers that the evidence does not support the charge or that for any reason the charge is not supportable, it should advise the accused to withdraw their plea and plead not guilty.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: When the prosecution accepts a plea, the court cannot reject it, unless it is not genuine or constitutes an abuse of process.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: ‘Those circumstances include ignorance, fear, duress, mistake or even the desire to gain a technical advantage’.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

refs.q: If the court considers the plea is not genuine it must either obtain an unequivocal plea or direct that a not guilty plea be entered.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.1 – Guilty plea > 2.3.1.1 – Acceptance of guilty plea

title: Depositions as sentencing material
statement: Depositions (committal transcript and statements, or the hand-up brief) are basic sentencing materials, need not be sworn or tested, and are reviewed broadly; conflicts with an agreed statement of facts should be raised with the parties; disputed items may be notified and evidence called. Depositions about admitted priors, or a co-offender’s depositions or record of interview where parity is in issue, should not be considered if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.

refs.q: Depositions consist of the transcript of the committal hearing and any statements accepted in evidence at that proceeding.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: However, if the depositions conflict with an agreed statement of facts, the court should raise the matter with the parties.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: should not be considered if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.

refs.q: The court may review depositions relating to prior convictions admitted by the offender or a co-offender’s depositions or records of interview if parity is in issue. These items can be used as evidence, are subject to objection (and hearing) by the defence and should not be considered if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: Where the committal proceeds by way of straight hand-up brief, the court uses the materials it contains in place of the traditional depositions.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: In Victoria, the practice is for the court to review depositions to broadly determine the nature of the offence without scrutinising them closely to exclude materials that might be inadmissible.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.2 – Depositions

refs.q: If any item in the depositions is disputed, the defence may notify the prosecution and the parties may then call evidence.

refs.q: As noted earlier, they are basic materials used in the sentencing process.

title: Mixed (State and federal) indictments
statement: Separate sentences must be imposed for State and federal charges and inconsistency avoided (e.g. a federal conditional release inconsistent with a State CCO); commencement dates and total terms need care. For the app: federal charges are outside its Victorian scope and must be flagged.

refs.q: A mixed indictment is one that charges both State and federal offences. A court must take care to ensure that separate sentences are imposed for the different charges. Any inconsistency must be avoided.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.1 – Mixed indictments

refs.q: Care must also be exercised in formulating orders which relate federal and State sentences to each other (for example commencement dates), and in indicating total terms of imprisonment where necessary.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.1 – Mixed indictments

title: Formulating sentence across multiple indictments
statement: The usual practice is to identify each indictment; impose sentences on each charge on each indictment with cumulation/concurrency orders within each indictment, then cumulation between indictments, then the non-parole period and other orders, and announce the result (e.g. base sentence on one indictment, part cumulative from another, total effective sentence).

refs.q: When formulating sentence, the usual practice is to impose sentences in relation to each charge on each indictment separately, along with associated orders for cumulation or concurrency that operate within the individual indictments, then formulate orders for cumulation between the indictments and finally specify a non-parole period or other associated orders.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.2 – Multiple indictments

refs.q: I direct that the sentence of 24 months on Indictment X be treated as the base sentence. I direct that 12 months of the sentence on Indictment Y be served cumulative upon the sentence imposed on Indictment X. This makes a total of 36 months imprisonment in respect of all offences for which you are presently before the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.3 – Formulation > 2.4.3.2 – Multiple indictments

title: Correction of errors in a sentence
statement: Courts have statutory and common law powers to correct errors (a clerical slip or an order not giving effect to the court’s intention, by supplemental order once recorded), but are functus officio once the order is recorded; s 104B reopening appears untested; alterations other than technical corrections should occur in open court with the parties heard.

refs.q: A court has broad powers, both statutorily and at common law, to correct errors in a sentence. However, it is functus officio once an order disposing of criminal proceedings has passed into the record of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors

refs.q: Every court has a power to correct any judgment or order that does not give effect to what the court intended, especially a clerical error.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.1 – Common law powers

refs.q: Because the sentencing process is a public part of the trial proceedings, any subsequent alteration (other than a technical correction per s 104A of the Act) should take place in open court with the parties being given an opportunity to be heard.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.1 – Common law powers

refs.q: If the order has passed into the record, the appropriate means of correction is to make a supplemental order.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.10 – Correction of errors > 2.4.10.1 – Common law powers
